Questions four and five. How do you design a CI CD pipeline for ML? And what is an evaluation gate, and why is it essential? The pipeline validates the new data, tests the feature transforms, trains on a versioned dataset, gates the result, promotes it in the registry, and rolls it out in stages: shadow, canary, full. Code, data or a schedule can trigger it, so new models arrive with nobody looking. The gate looks for you: the candidate must beat the production model on a fixed holdout set, or the build fails. Without it, a retrain can quietly ship a regression. The follow-up is what beat means. Simulate a retrain on last month's data, which held almost none of one customer group. The candidate wins overall, seventy-seven percent to seventy-five. On that group, one customer in twenty, it falls from seventy-nine percent to forty-six, worse than a coin flip. So the gate also sets a floor on every slice that matters, not just the total.

Question six. How do you monitor a model in production? In two layers. Operational health: latency at the median and the tail, error rate, throughput and resources. Model health: the input feature distributions, the distribution of predictions, and once labels arrive, live accuracy, precision and recall. Log inputs and predictions, so you can debug and replay, and wire every alert to an action: retrain, or roll back. Labels can take weeks, so the inputs and the predictions are what you'll see move first. That's where drift comes in.
